header.sourceTrackerNote: SHA-256 of the external tracker as migrated. Recorded so a later copy can be compared rather than assumed identical.

purpose: Records modifications to IMMUTABLE UPLOADED SOURCES. Such a source is never edited in place — the file as uploaded is preserved exactly, and every change to its content is recorded here instead. An overlay entry is therefore the authoritative statement of what a source now says, layered over what it originally said.
whyOverlaysRatherThanEdits: An uploaded source is evidence of what was provided and when. Editing it in place destroys that evidence and makes it impossible to tell an original requirement from a later reinterpretation. The overlay keeps both: the source stays as received, and the modification carries its own date, author, and reason.
readingRule: An immutable source MUST be read together with every ACTIVE overlay targeting it. Reading the source alone yields a stale answer, and in at least one case an actively wrong one: the DDR file contains no occurrence of D-67, D-68, or the D-47 field name event_sequence_num. All three exist ONLY as overlays. Where an overlay and its source conflict, the overlay wins.
targetsNotHeldInThisRepository: The 500-series sources are uploaded artifacts and are not committed here. An overlay does not require its target to be co-located; it requires the target to be identified unambiguously. Each entry therefore records the target's SHA-256 as it stood when the overlay was written, so a future reader can tell whether the source has since changed underneath the overlay. A hash mismatch is not automatically an error — it means the overlay must be re-read against the newer source before being trusted.

overlays.hashNote: SHA-256 of the copy available at authoring time. Recorded so drift between source and overlay is detectable rather than silent.
overlays.modification: Source-system options offered to a client MUST NOT imply that Microsoft Fabric is unsupported as a client data source. A client lakehouse is a legitimate source, on the same footing as CSV, Excel, and a database or table export.
overlays.appliesTo: Phase 0 (Intake & prerequisites) and Phase 2 (Data assessment & Event-Log Contract), wherever source systems or delivery formats are discussed with the client.
overlays.reason: Microsoft Fabric is excluded as a DEPLOYMENT TARGET for ProjectOne, because Fabric Warehouse cannot enforce uniqueness constraints and so cannot satisfy LOCKED decision D-62. That exclusion is about where ProjectOne runs. It says nothing about where a client's data may come from, and the two are easy to conflate. A practitioner who has absorbed 'Fabric is out' may decline a legitimate integration on the strength of a decision that does not apply to it.
overlays.commercialNote: Mid-market and enterprise clients increasingly land data in Fabric. Treating it as unsupported would forgo a commercial advantage that costs nothing architecturally — the data contract is the boundary, and source technology sits outside it.
overlays.guidanceForPractitioners: When a client says their data is in Fabric, the answer is yes. A Fabric lakehouse export is one more source shape behind the same event-log contract. Nothing about the contract changes.
overlays.acceptanceTest: Any statement of source-system options in 502, whether in the playbook or in derived client-facing material, must either list Fabric among acceptable sources or be silent about it. It must never present Fabric as unsupported or out of scope.

overlays.hashNote: SHA-256 of the copy available at authoring time.
overlays.status_explanation: RECORDED NOW, APPLIED LATER — and the distinction is deliberate. FR-006 carries an explicit timing constraint: 'Post-MVP — when connector work is scoped, not before.' Applying this overlay today would advertise a connector capability that does not exist, in a client-facing document. Leaving it unrecorded until then would rely on memory, which is the failure the forward requirements register exists to prevent. So the obligation is recorded with its trigger, and remains PENDING until the trigger fires.
overlays.modificationWhenTriggered: In §8 (Format & delivery), a Fabric lakehouse should be listed among candidate source shapes, alongside CSV, Excel, and a database or table export. §8 currently reads: 'Format: CSV, Excel, or a database/table export. (Direct API ingestion comes later.)'
overlays.reason: The data contract is the boundary; source technology sits outside it. A Fabric lakehouse is one more source shape behind the same contract, requiring no change to what the contract asks for.
overlays.acceptanceTest: Once the trigger has fired: §8 of 504 lists a Fabric lakehouse among candidate source shapes. Until then, this entry's correct state is PENDING, and a reviewer finding it PENDING has found the intended state, not an omission.
overlays.doNotApplyEarly: Marking this ACTIVE before connector work is scoped would put an unsupported capability in front of a client. The PENDING state is the requirement being met, not deferred.

overlays.verbatimEntry:
Add the Data-Driven Theming Architecture as the next DDR decision

**Target document:** `201-ProjectOne-Design-Decision-Record.md`  
**Snapshot:** Version 1.37, D-01 through D-66  
**Location:** Decision summary table immediately after D-66; detailed-decision section immediately after “D-66 detail”  
**Change type:** INSERT AFTER  
**Status:** APPROVED — EFFECTIVE OVERLAY  
**Approval:** John explicitly approved the theming requirement, 2026-08-05

**Current anchor text:**

> | D-66 | **Process-mining analytics: native implementation, no PM4Py — conformance is rule-based; log-skeleton + temporal-profile harvested as a native RULE-MINING engine ...** |

**Prescribed decision-summary insertion:**

> | D-67 | **Data-Driven Theming Architecture — design-token system plus runtime Theming/Skinning Engine.** ProjectOne stores theme definitions in a platform-agnostic, versioned format such as JSON; validates and resolves primitive, semantic, component, state, and visualization tokens; and maps approved resolved tokens directly to CSS Custom Properties for the web client. Runtime skinning and wholesale appearance replacement must not require feature-code changes or embed feature behavior in the theme layer. The architecture includes inheritance, fallback, compatibility, tenant-safe resolution, rollback, accessibility validation, and persistent theme regression. | LOCKED | Owner |

**Prescribed detailed insertion:**

> **D-67 detail — Data-Driven Theming Architecture.** ProjectOne uses a Design Token-Based Theming System and a Theming/Skinning Engine. Canonical theme data is stored in a platform-agnostic, versioned format such as JSON. The canonical flow is: theme data → schema validation → primitive/semantic/component/state/visualization token resolution → Theming/Skinning Engine → platform adapter → CSS Custom Properties for the web UI.
>
> Feature slices consume approved semantic or component tokens and approved themed shared controls. They do not create private theme systems, hard-code replacement appearance values where approved tokens exist, or place feature business logic in the theme layer.
>
> Runtime skinning supports approved tenant, product, environment, branding, density, and accessibility skins when authorized. The system defines precedence, inheritance, fallback, safe defaults, invalid-theme containment, cache behavior, persistence, auditability, rollback, compatibility, and tenant isolation.
>
> Wholesale appearance replacement may alter approved color, typography, spacing within compatible limits, radius, shadow, iconography, density, chart palette, and component treatment. It may not silently change workflow steps, control meaning, data semantics, navigation, permissions, required accessibility behavior, validation, analytical meaning, or functional visibility.
>
> Every theme and theme-engine change requires applicable schema, completeness, mapping, visual, shared-control, accessibility, responsive, visualization-readability, performance, isolation, persistence, fallback, and rollback tests. Higher-risk token-schema or engine changes may require full GUI, functional, supported-environment, accessibility, and performance portfolios.

**Reason:** This is a platform design decision and must be represented in the effective DDR.

overlays.verbatimEntry:
Add D-68 business-unit assignment precedence for `event.business_unit_key`

**Target document:** `201-ProjectOne-Design-Decision-Record.md`  
**Snapshot:** Version 1.37, plus effective D-67 overlay  
**Location:** Decision summary immediately after effective D-67; detailed decision immediately after effective D-67 detail  
**Change type:** INSERT AFTER  
**Status:** APPROVED — EFFECTIVE OVERLAY  
**Approval:** PBGCA-011-A* explicitly approved by John, 2026-08-08

**Prescribed summary row:**

> | D-68 | **Event business-unit assignment precedence (resolves OI-1).** When a valid direct event business-unit value is supplied and mapped, it is authoritative for that event and populates effective `event.business_unit_key`. Otherwise derive the effective business unit from `resource_dim.business_unit_key` **as-of `event.from_ts`** using SCD-2 history. Record assignment provenance. When both direct and resource-derived values exist and disagree, keep the valid direct event value as effective, set a conflict flag, and surface the disagreement as a data-quality finding rather than silently overwriting either meaning. | LOCKED | Owner + PBGCA remediation |

**Prescribed D-68 detail:**

> **D-68 detail — event business-unit assignment precedence.**
>
> 1. **Direct wins when valid.** If the event-log mapping supplies a business-unit value that resolves to a valid `business_unit_dim` member for the tenant, that value represents the event context and becomes effective `event.business_unit_key`.
> 2. **Resource is the deterministic fallback.** If no valid direct event business unit is available, derive `business_unit_key` from the event's resolved `resource_dim.business_unit_key` using the resource SCD-2 version valid at `event.from_ts`. Never use the resource's current business unit for a historical event.
> 3. **Provenance is mandatory.** Record `business_unit_assignment_source` as `direct_event`, `resource_asof`, or `none`.
> 4. **Disagreement is a finding, not an overwrite.** When a valid direct value and a resource-derived value both exist and differ, retain the direct event value as effective, set `business_unit_conflict_flag = true`, and emit an explicit data-quality/reconciliation finding. The raw direct source value remains recoverable in the event `attributes` payload; the resource-derived value remains reproducible from SCD-2 resource history.
> 5. **Invalid direct values do not silently win.** An unresolvable direct value is a validation finding; if a valid resource-as-of value exists it may supply the effective key with `business_unit_assignment_source = resource_asof`.
> 6. **No silent defaulting.** If neither path resolves, `event.business_unit_key` remains NULL and the missing enrichment is visible to affected analyses.
> 7. The machine-readable field definitions live in `ProjectOne-Field-Catalog-Registry-v1.0.json`.

**Reason:** Two builds must not assign different business units to the same event, and historical resource movement must not rewrite past event context.

overlays.approval: D69-A approved by John, 2026-08-24. Explicit approval following review of the drafted decision.

overlays.reason: The canon has no coding-practice layer. Across all 35 Project documents there are zero occurrences of 'functional core', 'imperative shell', 'pure function', 'side-effect', 'dependency inversion', 'cohesion', 'loosely coupled' or 'stateless'. P-1..P-9 are design principles; the D-decisions govern schema, serving, cloud and vocabulary. Nothing governs how code is structured. Meanwhile AC-MINING-PLACEMENT requires mining in SQL, which a naive reading of functional-core purity directly contradicts.
overlays.prescribedSummaryRow: | D-69 | **Code structure and computation placement — Functional Core / Imperative Shell, with the analytical tier carved out.** Application and domain logic follows a Functional Core / Imperative Shell model: business rules are deterministic, side-effect-free functions; I/O, database access, network, filesystem, messaging, logging, system time, randomness and environment access are isolated behind explicit interfaces; state is explicit, never hidden in globals; dependencies are injected, not reached for. **The analytical tier is deliberately OUTSIDE the functional core and is governed by AC-MINING-PLACEMENT.** Placement of any computation over event data is decided by two questions, in order: (1) does the input grow with tenant data volume? If yes, it executes set-based in SQL — no exception. (2) If the input is bounded by result shape rather than data volume, SQL remains the default; Python is used only where SQL genuinely cannot express the operation. Mining executes as a scheduled or background job that materializes results the API reads, never in-request. | LOCKED | Owner |
overlays.prescribedDetail:
**D-69 detail — code structure and computation placement.**

**Scope.** The Functional Core / Imperative Shell model governs application and domain logic — tenant routing, authorization, request validation, configuration resolution, response shaping, orchestration. Most of the codebase. There is no tension with AC-MINING-PLACEMENT in any of it.

The carve-out applies to ONE thing: computation over event data. Applying it more widely is a misreading.

**Why a carve-out is needed at all.** Under Functional Core / Imperative Shell a SQL query is I/O, and therefore shell rather than core. Under AC-MINING-PLACEMENT the mining logic IS SQL, by design. An agent given both rules without this decision will resolve the conflict by pulling mining into Python to make it pure — which is precisely the failure AC-MINING-PLACEMENT exists to prevent, and it will look like good practice while doing it.

**THE TWO QUESTIONS.** Asked in order, for any computation over event data.

**Question 1 — does the input grow with tenant data volume?**

- YES → executes set-based in SQL. No exception, no argument, regardless of the operation.
- NO → Python is permitted; proceed to Question 2.

"Every event" grows. "One row per activity" does not — a process has a bounded activity count whether the tenant loads ten thousand events or ten million. The test is answerable at design time by reading a function signature. It requires no profiler, no benchmark, and no production data, which matters because none exists yet.

The operative variable is INPUT CARDINALITY, not algorithmic complexity. The dominant cost is data movement, not computation (CP-002). An O(n log n) sort is fine in either place; moving four million rows across a process boundary to perform it is not.

**Question 2 — can SQL express the operation?**

- YES → use SQL anyway. SQL is the default, not the fallback.
- NO → Python.

SQL is inadequate for the following classes. THIS ENUMERATION IS ILLUSTRATIVE OF THE OBJECTIVE, NOT A DEFINITION OF IT. The objective is: SQL unless SQL genuinely cannot do the work.

1. Unbounded-depth recursion through cyclic structures — recursive CTEs are row-at-a-time and cycle handling degrades badly
2. Iterative convergence, where termination depends on a convergence criterion rather than on data
3. Sequence alignment and edit-distance computation
4. Linear algebra and matrix operations
5. Combinatorial search and optimization

The iterative-convergence exception is bounded: permitted only when the iteration count is determined by convergence or a parameter, NEVER by data size, AND the input already satisfies Question 1. An algorithm that iterates over event rows is row-wise Python wearing a hat.

**What SQL handles well — reaching for Python here is the common error.** Directly-follows pairs (LAG within case partition), variant identification (STRING_AGG then group), percentiles and quantiles (PERCENTILE_CONT), running totals, rank, gap-and-island, sessionization (window functions), conformance rule evaluation (set predicates), wait-time and bottleneck aggregation (group-by with window diff). Native regex is generally available in Azure SQL Database; pattern matching does not by itself justify moving work to Python.

**The dangerous quadrant.** An operation that is BOTH SQL-inadequate AND has data-volume-bound input — sequence alignment across all traces, for example. The answer is never "therefore Python." It is: reduce first in SQL, then apply Python to the reduced set. Align over the bounded variant set, not over every trace. If reduction is genuinely impossible, that is an escalation, not a judgment call.

**Timing is an independent requirement.** Mining executes as a scheduled or background job that materializes results the API reads. Correct SQL inside a request handler still violates the constraint. Both the placement rule and the timing rule must hold.

**Runtime backstop.** Every Python analytical entry point asserts its input size against a declared row budget and FAILS LOUDLY when exceeded. This catches the case where a cardinality assumed bounded turns out not to be for a pathological process. It is an assertion in code, not a design-time threshold — design-time thresholds are untestable before data exists and invite argument afterwards.

**When the rule does not clearly decide.** Raise a DECISION_REQUIRED escalation under the role contract. Do not choose. Every such escalation is evidence that this decision needs tightening, and is more useful recorded than resolved silently.

**Functional Core / Imperative Shell, stated for the application tier.**

- Domain and business logic: deterministic, side-effect-free functions wherever practical
- Side effects — database, network, filesystem, messaging, logging, system time, randomness, environment access — isolated behind explicit interfaces or adapters
- State explicit, intentionally scoped, never hidden in globals or implicit runtime behaviour
- Dependencies declared and injected; business logic depends on abstractions, not on infrastructure
- Application and service layers stateless wherever practical

**Relationship to existing decisions and controls.** D-69 does not restate rules already enforced elsewhere, and must not be read as superseding them. Slice boundaries and cross-slice contracts are enforced by check_slice_boundaries.py (VSA-1/VSA-3). Bounded change surface is enforced per pull request (CPM-1). Dependency pinning and reproducibility are enforced by the technology registry and the committed lockfile. Determinism of chart output is governed by the chart ground rules. Idempotency of re-load is governed by D-62 at the storage layer. Where D-69 and an existing control appear to overlap, the existing control governs and D-69 is context.

overlays.approval: D70-A approved by John, 2026-08-25. Option B selected after review of three options and their costs.

overlays.reason: D-49 explicitly left the date/period dimension shape open within R-4. F1a builds Tier-1 serving and, per D-49, a date dimension. Building it without the clock rule settled means either omitting the shape — a deferred DESIGN, which P-8 forbids — or storing a derived value that a calendar change invalidates.
overlays.prescribedSummaryRow: | D-70 | **Period/date dimension shape and the dual-clock rule — closes the R-4 remainder.** A date/period dimension carries per-tenant working hours, holidays and fiscal-calendar attributes. Duration may be read on either a CALENDAR clock or a BUSINESS clock, selected at read time as a parameter. **No business-clock duration is ever stored on a fact.** Business duration is derived at read time by set-based join against the calendar dimension; only raw timestamps and calendar duration are stored. | LOCKED | Owner |
overlays.prescribedDetail:
**D-70 detail — period/date dimension shape and the dual-clock rule.**

**What this closes.** D-49 recorded: *"Still open within R-4: the shape of the date/period dimension (business-hours vs calendar SLA clock; per-tenant fiscal calendar)."* This closes that half. The CR-5 item-3 metric-catalog home remains open and is unaffected.

**The rule.**

1. A date/period dimension carries, per tenant: working-hours definition, holiday calendar, timezone, and fiscal-calendar attributes.
2. Any duration may be read on a **calendar clock** or a **business clock**. The clock is a **read-time parameter**, not a stored property.
3. **No business-clock duration is stored on a fact.** Only raw timestamps and calendar duration are stored.
4. Business duration is derived at read time by **set-based join** against the calendar dimension — never row-wise, per D-69.

**Why storing business duration is prohibited.** A business-clock duration is derived from a MUTABLE input: the tenant's calendar. Add a public holiday and every stored value covering that date becomes wrong. Correcting them means rewriting derived values across live data — the migration DDR P-8 exists to prevent.

Computing at read time inverts the failure: adding a holiday changes future answers and leaves history intact, because history is recomputed from timestamps that never moved.

This is the same shape as chart ground rule 15 — store additive components, compute the derived value at the last step so re-aggregation stays arithmetically correct. A stored business duration is a pre-divided rate.

**Two distinct concerns in one dimension.** Business-hours affects DURATIONS. Fiscal calendar affects PERIOD GROUPING — which quarter a date falls in. Different columns, different risk, same dimension. Neither is stored on a fact.

**Worked illustration.** A repair triaged Friday 16:00 and completed Monday 10:00, against a two-day SLA. Calendar clock: 66 hours, 2.75 days, BREACHED. Business clock at 09:00–17:00 Mon–Fri: one hour Friday plus one hour Monday, two hours, MET. Same two stored timestamps; the weekend is the entire difference. A platform that can only report the first misrepresents the performance of any client whose SLA is quoted in business days.

**Reach beyond the schema.** Chart spec 203 records R-4 as *"Blocking for business-clock use. The chart is insulated; the data layer cannot emit business-clock offsets until R-4 lands."* The chart renders whatever offsets it receives. This decision unblocks the data layer that supplies them.

**Known and accepted risk.** Read-time computation must fit the Tier-1 sub-second budget (D-26). It is a join-and-sum against a calendar dimension — set-based, satisfying D-69 — but UNMEASURED, because no data exists at volume. If measurement later shows a specific query missing the budget, the remedy is a TARGETED materialization for that query, which D-49 already characterises as additive rather than schema rework. The remedy must not become storing business duration on the fact generally; that would reintroduce the mutable-derived-value problem this decision exists to avoid.

**What F1a must build.** A date/period dimension shaped to carry per-tenant working-hours, holiday and fiscal-calendar attributes. The attributes may be unpopulated at F1a — the SHAPE may not be deferred, per P-8. No duration column on any fact may be business-clock derived.
